approachQuestion.prompt:
Queue Preparation
Rearrange a mutable array into any valid binary min-heap in the same array. A parent must be at most both existing children. You need not sort the values or return a second array. Example: [5,2,4,1] may become [1,2,4,5].

0 ≤ n ≤ 200000; signed 32-bit values, with duplicates allowed. Preserve every occurrence. Use the supplied storage and only constant additional workspace. Which approach best meets this contract?
constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 200000; signed 32-bit values, with duplicates allowed. Preserve every occurrence. Use the supplied storage and only constant additional workspace.

options.text: Visit internal nodes from the last parent back to the root. At each node, iteratively sift its value down by exchanging with the smaller child until its subtree satisfies heap order.
options.feedback: Children’s subtrees are already heaps when a parent is processed. Most nodes are close to leaves, so the aggregate repair work is smaller than inserting every value independently.

options.text: Treat each growing prefix as a heap, and sift the newly included final value upward before extending the prefix.
options.feedback: This builds a valid heap in place but can repeatedly move new values through the full prefix height.

options.text: Iteratively heapsort the array into nondecreasing order in place.
options.feedback: A sorted array is a valid min-heap, but complete sorting imposes unnecessary ordering.

options.text: Process internal nodes from root toward the leaves, sifting each down once without revisiting earlier nodes.
options.feedback: For [9,8,7,6,5,4,3], a full root sift first gives [7,8,3,6,5,4,9]. Processing node 1 next gives [7,5,3,6,8,4,9]; node 2 needs no change. The root 7 still exceeds child 3.

Repair children before parents so every sift starts above already valid subheaps. Most nodes are near leaves and have very short possible sifts; charging log n to all nodes loses the linear height-sum bound.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze A using iterative sift-down, processing all internal nodes from right to left. Let n be array length. No copied array, recursive calls, or returned new array is used. Choose the tightest time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Use the tightest worst-case bound for the whole input unless amortized or expected accounting is explicitly specified. Comparing or moving a record and arithmetic on machine words take constant time.

Exclude supplied input and returned output from auxiliary space. Count working arrays, queues, tables and call stacks. Output storage is separate and is not used as workspace. Heap repairs and traversals are iterative. No hashing is used unless explicitly stated.

options.text: O(n log(n+1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Summing repairs by node height gives linear bottom-up heap construction.
details: There are at most n/2 nodes of height at least one, n/4 of height at least two, and so on. Summing repair work over heights gives O(n), tight for inputs needing changes across a linear number of nodes. Iterative swaps use O(1) workspace and modify the supplied array directly.
“O(n log(n+1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Multiplying all nodes by maximum height is loose; few nodes have that height.
“O(n) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: The supplied array is input storage and no auxiliary heap is allocated.
“O(log(n+1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: One sift is height-bounded, but preparation visits a linear number of internal nodes.
